species.name: Ghost Ant
species.fact: The most common kitchen ant in South Florida — colonies split into many satellite nests, which is why sprays seem to make more of them.
species.note: One trail is a bait job; trails every week mean nests in the walls.

species.name: Bigheaded Ant
species.fact: The big-headed workers are the colony’s "soldiers" — those jaws crack seeds, not skin.
species.note: Mostly a paver/foundation nuisance, but supercolonies get enormous without treatment.

species.name: Red Imported Fire Ant
species.fact: Workers grip with their jaws and pivot to sting multiple times — and they cue on movement, so they tend to sting all at once.
species.note: With kids or pets in the yard, mounds are worth treating properly — kicking them just relocates the colony.

species.name: Florida Carpenter Ant
species.fact: They don’t eat wood like termites — they hollow out damp or damaged wood to nest, so finding them often means finding a moisture problem.
species.note: The ants are manageable; the moisture-damaged wood they chose is the real finding.

species.name: Tawny Crazy Ant
species.fact: They’re notorious for swarming into electrical boxes and equipment — and they displace even fire ants where they establish.
species.note: Numbers make DIY hopeless; infestations are measured in millions.

species.name: White-footed Ant
species.fact: Colonies can hold a million-plus ants, and most workers never leave the nest — which is why the trail you kill keeps coming back.
species.note: Harmless but famously persistent; exterior treatment beats kitchen-counter sprays.

species.name: Subterranean Termite
species.fact: The mud tubes are climate-controlled highways — termites dry out fast, so they build covered roads between soil and wood.
species.note: Termite damage is rarely covered by homeowners insurance. Tubes or swarmers = inspection time.

species.name: Drywood Termite
species.fact: Those pellet piles are "kick-out" debris — the colony sweeps its gallery and pushes the pellets out a hole the size of a pin.
species.note: Pellets mean an active colony in that wood member. Early treatment is far cheaper than late.

species.name: Formosan Termite
species.fact: A mature Formosan colony can hold millions — they’re called "super termites" for colony size, not bite.
species.note: The most destructive termite in Florida. Swarms near your lights justify an inspection.

species.name: American Cockroach
species.fact: The classic Florida "palmetto bug." It lives outdoors in mulch, palms, and sewers — one in the house is a visitor, not an infestation.
species.note: Occasional wanderers are weather-driven. Nightly sightings mean an entry point or moisture source worth fixing.

species.name: German Cockroach
species.fact: This one never lives outdoors in Florida — it arrives in bags, boxes, and used appliances. It’s a hitchhiker, not a cleanliness verdict.
species.note: The fastest-breeding indoor roach. Foggers scatter them deeper — baiting programs work.

species.name: Smokybrown Cockroach
species.fact: Dries out easily, so it follows moisture — clogged gutters are a favorite address.
species.note: Porch-light visitors are normal; attic activity is worth addressing.

species.name: Yellow Fever Mosquito
species.fact: It doesn’t need a pond — a plant saucer after one afternoon storm raises a generation in about a week.
species.note: Day-biting around the patio = container breeding within ~150 feet. Tip the water first; treatment handles the rest.

species.name: Asian Tiger Mosquito
species.fact: Arrived in the US in the 1980s in shipments of used tires — the world’s most-traveled mosquito.
species.note: Same playbook: eliminate standing water, then treat resting areas.

species.name: No-See-Um
species.fact: They’re small enough to pass through regular 16-mesh screening — coastal homes use finer "no-see-um mesh" for a reason.
species.note: Miserable but not a home infestation issue — timing, fans, and finer screens are the real fixes.

species.name: Lovebug
species.fact: They don’t bite or sting at all — but their body residue is mildly acidic and can mark car paint if baked on for days.
species.note: A car-wash problem, not a pest-control problem. They’re gone in a few weeks.

species.name: Southern Chinch Bug
species.fact: The #1 killer of St. Augustine lawns in Florida. The tell: drought stress recovers with water, chinch damage doesn’t.
species.note: They kill outward from the first patch — early treatment saves the lawn, late means resodding.

species.name: Mole Cricket
species.fact: Males sing from burrows they shape like megaphones to amplify the call across the neighborhood.
species.note: Tunneling severs roots — small areas recover, spreading tunnels need treatment.

species.name: Tropical Sod Webworm
species.fact: The moths do zero damage — it’s their caterpillars feeding at night that shear the lawn.
species.note: Late-summer classic. Treated early, the lawn regrows quickly.

species.name: Fall Armyworm
species.fact: The name is literal — they advance across turf in fronts, eating as they go.
species.note: Fast movers. The birds found them before you did.

species.name: White Grub
species.fact: Animal digging is usually the first sign — the grubs are the buffet, your lawn is the tablecloth.
species.note: Fix the grubs and the diggers have less reason to stick around — not a guarantee, but the right first move.

species.name: Twolined Spittlebug
species.fact: The "spit" is a bubble tent the nymph builds around itself for moisture and protection.
species.note: Light foam is cosmetic; widespread stripes-and-foam plus browning is treatable.

species.name: Eastern Lubber Grasshopper
species.fact: Its colors are a warning label — lubbers are toxic enough that most predators spit them back out.
species.note: Toxic enough to make a pet sick if eaten — keep pets away, vet if one does. Defensive foam irritates skin and eyes, so don’t handle them; ornamental damage is rarely severe.

species.name: Golden Silk Orb-weaver
species.fact: Her silk is, weight-for-weight, tougher than steel — and she rebuilds the web’s damaged sections nightly.
species.note: Eats mosquitoes and flies all day. Relocate the web if it’s across your walkway; don’t kill the engineer.

species.name: Wolf Spider
species.fact: Mothers carry their spiderlings piggyback — dozens riding shotgun. It’s the only spider that does this.
species.note: Free roach and cricket control. Scoop-and-release beats squishing.

species.name: Huntsman Spider
species.fact: A dedicated cockroach hunter — one huntsman on patrol is a roach’s worst night.
species.note: Terrifying-looking, essentially harmless, genuinely useful. The scream is optional.

species.name: Brown Widow
species.fact: Now more common than black widows in much of Florida — but notably shyer and less prone to bite.
species.note: Respect, don’t panic. Gloves when moving stored patio furniture; treat if egg sacs multiply.

species.name: Southern Black Widow
species.fact: Bites are rare and defensive — nearly all happen when a hand reaches blind into her hiding spot.
species.note: The one Florida spider worth professional attention when found where kids or pets play.

species.name: Roof Rat
species.fact: Florida’s aerialist — it runs fences and branches like a tightrope walker and enters at roofline, not floor level.
species.note: Attic noise + chewed wires is an urgent combination. Exclusion (sealing entries) is the permanent fix.

species.name: Norway Rat
species.fact: Ground-floor specialist — where roof rats take the high road, Norways dig in at the foundation.
species.note: Burrow + droppings = established. Trapping plus entry sealing, in that order.

species.name: House Mouse
species.fact: A mouse nibbles at 20–30 food sites a night rather than one big meal — which is why droppings show up everywhere at once.
species.note: One mouse is rarely one mouse. Seal dime-sized gaps or the next one uses the same door.

species.name: Cat Flea
species.fact: Adults on the pet are ~5% of the infestation — the other 95% is eggs, larvae, and pupae in carpet and bedding.
species.note: Pet treatment alone loses. Home + yard + pet together, timed to the life cycle, wins.

species.name: Brown Dog Tick
species.fact: The only tick that can complete its entire life cycle indoors — an infestation can live in the house itself.
species.note: Indoor ticks are a program, not a one-off spray. Coordinate with your vet on pet treatment.

species.name: Bed Bug
species.fact: They follow luggage and furniture, not filth — five-star hotels get them too. Clean homes are not immune.
species.note: DIY sprays scatter them to neighboring rooms. Inspection first, then targeted treatment.

species.name: Paper Wasp
species.fact: They hunt caterpillars all day to feed their young — a nest away from doors is quietly working your garden.
species.note: Leave nests you can ignore; remove the ones over doorways (early morning, or have us do it).

species.name: Mud Dauber
species.fact: She stocks each mud cell with paralyzed spiders for her young — including widows. A spider-control subcontractor.
species.note: Almost never stings. Scrape old tubes off; that’s the whole job.

species.name: Yellowjacket
species.fact: A hidden ground nest can hold thousands by fall — the lawnmower usually finds it first.
species.note: Ground nests near activity areas are the definition of a professional job.

species.name: Honey Bee (swarm)
species.fact: One worker bee makes about 1/12 of a teaspoon of honey in her lifetime — a swarm is house-hunting, not attacking.
species.note: Swarms usually move on within days. A local beekeeper can collect them free — don’t spray pollinators.

species.name: Honey Bee (wall colony)
species.fact: A wall colony builds comb fast — and sealing the entrance traps bees inside, where dying comb leaks honey into the wall.
species.note: Needs prompt bee-friendly removal (comb out, cavity cleaned). Never just plug the hole.

species.name: Carpenter Bee
species.fact: That intimidating hovering guard is a male with no stinger — pure bluff.
species.note: A hole or two is cosmetic; years of re-drilling plus woodpecker follow-up damage adds up. Paint is the best prevention.

species.name: Puss Caterpillar
species.fact: The most venomous caterpillar in the United States hides under that fur — the "hairs" conceal venomous spines.
species.note: Never touch; teach kids the "cute = don’t" rule. Stings are intensely painful but rarely dangerous.

species.name: Io Moth Caterpillar
species.fact: It grows into a moth with huge false "eyes" on its hindwings — one of Florida’s prettiest transformations from one of its spiciest caterpillars.
species.note: Spines sting like nettles. Look, photograph, don’t pet.

species.name: Silverfish
species.fact: Silverfish are older than dinosaurs — they were doing this exact job 100 million years before T. rex.
species.note: Mostly a storage-box nuisance. Lots of them signals a humidity problem worth fixing.

species.name: Earwig
species.fact: The pincers are for folding its wings and courtship — the ear thing is pure medieval myth.
species.note: Fix door sweeps and drainage; the visitors stop themselves.

species.name: Florida Ivory Millipede
species.fact: A composting machine — it recycles dead leaves into soil. Rain floods the leaf litter and evicts them onto your lanai.
species.note: They can’t survive indoors — sweep them out or wait; they dry out in a day.

species.name: House Centipede
species.fact: It actively hunts roaches, silverfish, and moths at night — an unpaid exterminator with too many legs.
species.note: If you can stand it, it’s working for you. If you can’t, cup-and-release counts.

species.name: Pillbug
species.fact: Not an insect at all — it’s a land crustacean that breathes through gill-like organs. A tiny armored shrimp cousin.
species.note: A drainage indicator more than a pest. Kids’ favorite yard animal.

species.name: Stink Bug
species.fact: The smell is a defense chemical from glands on its thorax — vacuum, don’t squish.
species.note: Seasonal wall-sitters. Sealing window gaps is the whole fix.

species.name: Drain Fly
species.fact: The larvae live in the gel film inside drains — which is why sprays fail and a stiff brush succeeds.
species.note: Clean the drain film (brush + enzyme cleaner) and they’re gone in days.

species.name: Fungus Gnat
species.fact: It’s an overwatering alarm with wings — the larvae need soggy soil to survive.
species.note: Let pots dry between waterings; yellow sticky cards catch the stragglers.

species.name: Cuban Treefrog
species.fact: An invasive that eats Florida’s smaller native treefrogs — one reason your porch chorus may have gone quiet.
species.note: Wash hands after contact. Turning porch lights off (or amber) removes the insect buffet that draws them.

species.name: Brown Anole
species.fact: The invasive cousin — it pushed Florida’s native green anole up into the trees. Look UP to find the green ones.
species.note: Eats enormous numbers of insects. The lanai’s volunteer security team.

species.name: House Gecko
species.fact: One of the few lizards with a voice — those evening chirps are territorial calls.
species.note: Night-shift bug patrol. The droppings on the windowsill are the rent.

species.name: Gopher Tortoise
species.fact: Its burrow shelters 350+ other species — Florida’s original landlord, and a protected species you’re lucky to host.
species.note: Protected by law — burrows can’t be disturbed. Mow around the apron and enjoy the neighbor.

species.name: Nine-banded Armadillo
species.fact: When startled it jumps straight up — a reflex that surprises people more than it protects the armadillo.
species.note: We don’t trap wildlife — a licensed trapper can remove it under FWC rules. It eats grubs and earthworms, so treating grubs helps but won’t reliably send it away; don’t handle it bare-handed.

species.name: Rugose Spiraling Whitefly
species.fact: The spiral pattern is her egg-laying signature — like a tiny crop circle under every frond.
species.note: Trees usually survive, but the sticky fallout zone makes treatment worth it.

species.name: Mealybug
species.fact: Ants literally farm them — guarding the herd and milking the honeydew like six-legged dairymen.
species.note: Small outbreaks wipe off with soapy water; recurring ones ride on the ant problem.

species.name: Aphid
species.fact: Aphids are born pregnant — generations telescope inside each other, which is how a clean plant is covered by Friday.
species.note: Blast with water, let the ladybugs work; treat only persistent infestations.

species.name: Tea Scale
species.fact: Adult scales never move again — they cement themselves down and live under armor for life.
species.note: Systemic treatment beats sprays — the armor sheds contact products.

species.name: Sri Lankan Weevil
species.fact: A newer Florida arrival that already feeds on 150+ plant species — the notched-leaf signature is everywhere.
species.note: Cosmetic on mature plants; young ornamentals may need protection.
